exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 1–6, solve the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ by using the $$LU$$ factorization given for $$A$$ ﻿. In Exercises 1 and 2, also solve $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ by ordinary row reduction.

Find an $$LU$$ factorization of the matrices in Exercises 7–16 (with $$L$$ unit lower triangular). Note that MATLAB will usually produce a permuted $$LU$$ factorization because it uses partial pivoting for numerical accuracy.

problem.paragraph: When $$A$$ is invertible, MATLAB finds $$A^{- 1}$$ by factoring $$A = LU$$ (where $$L$$ may be permuted lower triangular), inverting $$L$$ and $$U$$ , and then computing $$U^{- 1}L^{- 1}$$ . Use this method to compute the inverse of $$A$$ in Exercise 2. (Apply the algorithm of Section 2.2 to $$L$$ and to $$U . \left.\right)$$
Find $$A^{- 1}$$ as in Exercise 17, using $$A$$ from Exercise 3.

Let $$A$$ be a lower triangular $$n \times n$$ matrix with nonzero entries on the diagonal. Show that $$A$$ is invertible and $$A^{- 1}$$ is lower triangular. [Hint: Explain why $$A$$ can be changed into $$I$$ using only row replacements and scaling. (Where are the pivots?) Also, explain why the row operations that reduce $$A$$ to $$I$$ change $$I$$ into a lower triangular matrix.]
Let $$A = LU$$ be an $$LU$$ factorization. Explain why $$A$$ can be row reduced to $$U$$ using only replacement operations. (This fact is the converse of what was proved in the text.)

Suppose $$A = BC$$ , where $$B$$ is invertible. Show that any sequence of row operations that reduces $$B$$ to $$I$$ also reduces $$A$$ to $$C$$ . The converse is not true, since the zero matrix may be factored as $$0 = B(0)$$ .﻿

exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 22–26 provide a glimpse of some widely used matrix factorizations, some of which are discussed later in the text.

problem.paragraph: (Reduced $$L U$$ Factorization) With $$A$$ as in the Practice Problem, find a $$5 \times 3$$ matrix $$B$$ and a $$3 \times 4$$ matrix $$C$$ such that $$A = BC$$ . Generalize this idea to the case where $$A$$ is $$m \times n$$ , $$A = LU$$ , and $$U$$ has only three nonzero rows.
(Rank Factorization) Suppose an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ admits a factorization $$A = CD$$ where $$C$$ is $$m \times 4$$ and $$D$$ is $$4 \times n$$ .﻿

list.item: Show that $$A$$ is the sum of four outer products. (See Section 2.4.)
Let $$m = 400$$ and $$n = 100$$ . Explain why a computer programmer might prefer to store the data from $$A$$ in the form of two matrices $$C$$ and $$D$$ .﻿

problem.paragraph: ( $$Q R$$ Factorization) Suppose $$A = QR$$ , where $$Q$$ and $$R$$ are $$n \times n$$ , $$R$$ is invertible and upper triangular, and $$Q$$ has the property that $$Q^{T}Q = I$$ . Show that for each $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has a unique solution. What computations with $$Q$$ and $$R$$ will produce the solution?

(Singular Value Decomposition) Suppose $$A = UDV^{T}$$ , where $$U$$ and $$V$$ are $$n \times n$$ matrices with the property that $$U^{T}U = I$$ and $$V^{T}V = I$$ , and where $$D$$ is a diagonal matrix with positive numbers $$\sigma_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\sigma_{n}$$ , on the diagonal. Show that $$A$$ is invertible, and find a formula for $$A^{- 1}$$ .﻿
(Spectral Factorization) Suppose a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix A admits a factorization as $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ , where $$P$$ is some invertible $$3 \times 3$$ matrix and $$D$$ is the diagonal matrix

$$D = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {1/2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1/3} \end{bmatrix}$$ Show that this factorization is useful when computing high powers of $$A$$ Find fairly simple formulas for $$A^{2}$$ , $$A^{3}$$ , and $$A^{k}$$ ( $$k$$ a positive integer), using $$P$$ and the entries in $$D$$ .﻿
Design two different ladder networks that each output $$9$$ volts and $$4$$ amps when the input is $$12$$ volts and $$6$$ amps.

Show that if three shunt circuits (with resistances $$R_{1}$$ , $$R_{2}$$ , $$R_{3}$$ ) are connected in series, the resulting network has the same transfer matrix as a single shunt circuit. Find a formula for the resistance in that circuit.

Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} {4/3} & {- 12} \\ {- 1/4} & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Design a ladder network whose transfer matrix is $$A$$ by finding a suitable matrix factorization of $$A$$ .﻿

problem.paragraph: Find a different factorization of the $$A$$ in Exercise 29, and thereby design a different ladder network whose transfer matrix is $$A$$ .﻿

[T] The solution to the steady-state heat flow problem for the plate in the figure is approximated by the solution to the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ , where $$\textbf{b} = (5,{15,0,10,0,10,20,30)}$$ and $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & - 1 & - 1 & & & & & \\ - 1 & 4 & 0 & - 1 & & & & \\ - 1 & 0 & 4 & - 1 & - 1 & & & \\ & - 1 & - 1 & 4 & 0 & - 1 & & \\ & & - 1 & 0 & 4 & - 1 & - 1 & \\ & & & - 1 & - 1 & 4 & 0 & - 1 \\ & & & & - 1 & 0 & 4 & - 1 \\ & & & & & - 1 & - 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$$

(Refer to Exercise 43 of Section 1.1.) The missing entries in $$A$$ are zeros. The nonzero entries of $$A$$ lie within a band along the main diagonal. Such band matrices occur in a variety of applications and often are extremely large (with thousands of rows and columns but relatively narrow bands).

list.item: Use the method of Example 2 to construct an $$LU$$ factorization of $$A$$ , and note that both factors are band matrices (with two nonzero diagonals below or above the main diagonal). Compute $$LU - A$$ to check your work.

Obtain $$A^{- 1}$$ and note that $$A^{- 1}$$ is a dense matrix with no band structure. When $$A$$ is large, $$L$$ and $$U$$ can be stored in much less space than $$A^{- 1}$$ . This fact is another reason for preferring the $$LU$$ factorization of $$A$$ to $$A^{- 1}$$ itself.

problem.paragraph: [T] The band matrix $$A$$ shown below can be used to estimate the unsteady conduction of heat in a rod when the temperatures at points $$p_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$p_{5}$$ , on the rod change with time.2

list.item: The constant $$C$$ in the matrix depends on the physical nature of the rod, the distance $$\text{Δ} x$$ between the points on the rod, and the length of time $$\text{Δ} t$$ between successive temperature measurements. Suppose that for $$k = 0$$ , $$1$$ , $$2$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\text{a}$$ vector $$\textbf{t}_{k}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{5}$$ lists the temperatures at time $$k \text{Δ} t$$ . If the two ends of the rod are maintained at $$0{^\circ}$$ , then the temperature vectors satisfy the equation $$A\textbf{t}_{k + 1} = \textbf{t}_{k}(k = 0,1,\ldots)$$ , where $$A = \left[\right. \left(\right. 1 + 2 C \left.\right) & - C & & & - C & \left(\right. 1 + 2 C \left.\right) & - C & & & - C & \left(\right. 1 + 2 C \left.\right) & - C & & & - C & \left(\right. 1 + 2 C \left.\right) & - C & & & - C & \left(\right. 1 + 2 C \left.\right) \left]\right.$$

Find the $$LU$$ factorization of $$A$$ when $$C = 1$$ , A matrix such as $$A$$ with three nonzero diagonals is called a tridiagonal matrix. The $$L$$ and $$U$$ factors are bidiagonal matrices. Suppose $$C = 1$$ and $$\textbf{t}_{0} = \left( 10,\left. 12,12,12,10 \right) \right.$$ . Use the $$LU$$ factorization of $$A$$ to find the temperature distributions $$\textbf{t}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{t}_{2}$$ , $$\textbf{t}_{3}$$ , and $$\textbf{t}_{4}$$ .﻿
